papers.title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
papers.abstract: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

papers.title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts.

papers.title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
papers.abstract: Background: Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse. Results: Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the Prunus dulcis Texas v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond. Conclusions: The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (fruitdbase.csic.es), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.

papers.title: Leakage-Controlled Benchmarking of Variant Effect Predictors and Development of Gradient-Boosting Consensus Model
papers.abstract: Single amino acid mutations are among the most common forms of genetic variation, with effects ranging from negligible to severe disruption of protein function. Accurate quantitative evaluation of protein variants therefore represents a key challenge in medicine and protein engineering. Computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) are widely used to prioritize missense variants, yet their fair comparison is hindered by data circularity, benchmarks restricted to human clinical annotations, and limited availability of code and training data, all of which can inflate apparent performance. Here, we reviewed 18 recent and 3 older, widely adopted variant effect predictors for reproducible benchmarking and assembled a rigorously curated, leakage-controlled Benchmark dataset by integrating clinically annotated human variants from ClinVar and Humsavar as well as cross-species variants with functional annotations. The evaluation on this dataset revealed a narrow overall performance range for the benchmarked tools (AUC 0.631-0.758) and a consistent drop from clinical to functional data. Surprisingly, several tools published two decades ago demonstrated comparable performance to mid-ranked modern predictors. Building on these results, we developed a gradient-boosting consensus model, PredictSNPprot, which achieved an AUC of 0.82 on a held-out test set, outperforming the original PredictSNP meta-predictor and the best individual state-of-the-art tool by 13.6 and 5.7 percentage points, respectively. The Benchmark dataset, including the predictions from the evaluated tools, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23597130 and PredictSNPprot consensus predictor is available at https://github.com/loschmidt/PredictSNPprot.

papers.title: Batch Effect Correction to Enhance Utility of a Publicly Available ALS Proteomics Dataset
papers.abstract: Large, publicly available databases of patient data have been successful in identifying associations between neurodegenerative diseases and biological features that might otherwise go unnoticed. The Answer ALS Consortium is one such database that has generated a rich repository of multi-omic data from people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, large studies can suffer from batch effects that obscure genuine biological signal and prevent experiment reproducibility. In this study, we identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS 1-2 proteomic dataset (508 samples x 3,643 proteins) and corrected the effect using both the internal controls provided by Answer ALS and the batch effect-correction algorithm (BECA) ComBat. We identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS Dataset 1-2 proteomic dataset that, uncorrected, may obscure biology. Proteins MOS and H4 were outliers of expression in the dataset that correlated with the batch effect. Removing MOS and H4 did not correct the effect fully but did reveal new principal component (PC) contributing proteins related to motor neurons and potentially ALS: AINX, NFL, and NFM. The batch differential controls (BDCs) provided by Answer ALS were used to correct samples in their respective batches. ComBat, a well-characterized BECA, was applied to the dataset both before (ComBat-BDC) and after (BDC-ComBat) correction with the BDCs. BDC-ComBat was the only method that successfully reduced batch effect across the entire dataset. This method also preserved four of the top six PC-contributing proteins from the original dataset, including three neuronal proteins, suggesting that the corrected dataset recapitulates biology as well as the variability of the original dataset. Altogether, we produced a version of the Answer ALS proteomic dataset (354 samples by 3,641 proteins) with globally reduced batch effect and protein-level reduced batch effect. This version of the dataset recapitulates the individual protein variability and important neuronal proteins of the original. We also created a workflow for identifying and correcting batch effects that can be applied to other large data repositories.

papers.title: Computational Repurposing of FDA Approved Drugs Against Cyclin Dependent Kinase (CDK2)
papers.abstract: Drug repurposing is an approach for identifying new therapeutic with existing FDA approved drugs. Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) is an important regulator of cell cycle progression. The present study aimed to identify FDA-approved drugs with potential binding activity against CDK2 using a Computational drug-repurposing approach. The crystal structure of Human CDK2 (PDB ID: 3PY0) was used for Molecular docking, followed by Protein Ligand Interaction Profiler (PLIP) analysis to evaluate Protein Ligand interactions. Further for drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic properties using Swiss ADME and for Predicted toxicity using ProTox Was done. Based on this docking affinity, interaction profiles, drug-likeness, pharmacokinetics and toxicity, the best target was selected. Carteolol demonstrated the most balanced overall computational profile and was selected as the primary candidate for potential computational finding to provide repurposing against CDK2. Experimental studies are required to validate its direct binding and inhibitory activity against CDK2.

papers.title: RNA assignment and segmentation geometry in Visium HD profiles of fibrostenotic Crohn's disease
papers.abstract: Retrospective reuse of spatial transcriptomics often starts from a deposited bin-level Seurat object rather than the inputs needed to revisit upstream molecular processing. We tested whether image segmentation could support a defensible cell-like reconstruction under this constraint in two complete H&E-stained intestinal sections from a Visium HD study of Crohn's disease-associated fibrostenosis (GSE302569). The available data comprised 18,085 genes, 988,942 original 8 {micro}m bins and 179,596,575 UMIs. We evaluated 20 segmentation configurations in the preserved image coordinate system using a common bin-centre assignment rule, without restarting Space Ranger or introducing higher-resolution expression. RNA assignment ranged from 0% to 74.68% in CD1 and 0% to 64.05% in CD2. Expansion increased recovery but did not eliminate merged regions, straight boundaries or within-bin ambiguity; approximately 70-73% of InstanSeg brightfield nuclear regions received no assigned RNA. All 38 non-empty configuration-slice combinations underwent native full-mode RCTD against the same nine-group scIBD reference. Mean slice-level RNA recovery was negatively associated with primary-component dominance across 19 configurations (descriptive Spearman {rho} = -0.77). Neither dominant-call agreement nor concentrated RCTD support validates boundaries or cell identity. The observed limitations in RNA recovery, region geometry, and compositional support did not establish any tested configuration as a reliable single-cell reconstruction from these inputs. The findings identify limitations of retrospective single-cell reconstruction from the available binned inputs, not the impossibility of cell-resolved analysis from suitable original data.

papers.title: Differentiable Spin-Center Diffusion Model Enables DEER-Guided Generative Pipeline of Weighted Protein Ensembles
papers.abstract: Biological function entails the interconversion of a protein between distinct conformations, an equilibrium modulated by ligands and other physicochemical conditions. Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy captures these ensembles as distance distributions, P(r), between spin label pairs. However, the width of P(r) convolves protein conformational heterogeneity with the rotameric flexibility of the label. Because current spin label models overestimate this contribution, translating P(r) into ensembles has remained indirect and predominantly qualitative. Here, we developed spin-center (SC) diffusion, a differentiable model of the spin label with a tunable spin label rotameric width. Coupled to a frozen Boltz-2 structure generator, SC diffusion enables the entire experimental P(r) to guide ensemble generation at inference time. We demonstrate the robustness of this pipeline on synthetic P(r) of known composition, recovering the ensemble populations, including both components of a bimodal profile. Guided by experimental P(r) measured under different biochemical conditions, ensembles of the transporters PfMATE, LmrP, MhsT and P-glycoprotein were modeled and free energy differences derived from the ensembles in a condition-dependent manner. By embedding a differentiable label model in structure generation, our approach interprets DEER distributions as weighted conformational ensembles, adding a missing thermodynamic grounding to generative protein structure prediction methods.

papers.title: The Findings Workflow: An agentic, collaborative, provenance-tracked framework for scientific data analysis with Claude Code
papers.abstract: Scientists presented with quantitative data often face two related problems: confidence that an analysis is statistically and computationally correct, and provenance sufficient to reproduce the resulting figures and conclusions. Large language models (LLMs) can make sophisticated analyses accessible through a collaborative, conversational interface, but unstructured use can worsen both problems by producing plausible but incorrect results and obscuring the steps that produced them. Here we present the Findings Workflow, a free, open-source Claude Code plugin designed to retain the flexibility of conversational LLM-assisted analysis while placing it within a structured, verifiable, and reproducible environment. The workflow uses staged, gated progression to ensure the science, metadata, and data are understood and tested data loaders are built before downstream analysis begins. Specialized subagents perform statistical analysis, programming, visualization, research, reporting, and validation, with independent review incorporated throughout. The plugin also provides vetted analysis templates, conventions, and methodological guidance that serve as trusted sources of opinion when deciding how analyses should be performed. Scientists remain actively involved throughout, exploring their data and directing the analysis through natural-language conversation, while the workflow supplies structure, verification, and persistent state around that collaboration. Findings are recorded automatically together with the data, code, methods, figures, and provenance needed to reproduce them. We demonstrate the workflow with a worked example that reproduces central findings from a published plasma extracellular vesicle proteomics dataset examining Alzheimer's disease (Mag-Net). Together, these features are designed to make LLM-assisted scientific analysis easier to trust, inspect, and reproduce without sacrificing its conversational and exploratory nature.

papers.title: ScanFold3: a robust and rapid approach for identifying structured RNA targets in genomes and transcriptomes
papers.abstract: Background. The rapid expansion of high-throughput transcriptomic datasets has created a critical need for scalable tools to identify functional RNA secondary structures. While thermodynamics-based folding is a well-established method, most algorithms lack the scalability required for genomic-scale datasets due to O(n3) time complexity. Methods. We present ScanFold3, an enhanced version of the ScanFold pipeline that optimizes the "Fold" step for modern computing needs. This version models consensus structure generation as a minimum perfect weighted matching problem on a graph. To ensure maximum scalability, we implemented a Greedy Approximation Algorithm and optimized performance-critical components in C++. Results. Benchmarking on sequences up to 128 kb demonstrates that ScanFold3 achieves a 38-fold to 129-fold increase in speed over ScanFold2. Validation against annotated human RNAs shows that ScanFold3 offers improved positive predictive value (PPV). Most significantly, when ScanFold3 outputs are used as structural constraints for global refolding, it outperforms previous versions across all metrics, including the F1 score. Conclusions. ScanFold3 provides a robust, speedy, and user-friendly method for characterizing the thermodynamics of novel RNA and DNA sequences. It is designed as an efficient first step for high throughput bioinformatic pipelines, capable of paring down chromosome-scale transcriptomic data into stable structures amenable to advanced analysis.

papers.title: Improving Molecular Docking Pose Recovery through Targeted Side-Chain Monte Carlo Sampling of an Apo Structure
papers.abstract: Receptor flexibility complicates molecular docking when only an unbound (apo) protein structure is available. Local side-chain rearrangements can alter binding-pocket accessibility and ligand complementarity, motivating approaches that sample these motions efficiently. Here, we evaluate a targeted Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) protocol that combines local and larger side-chain torsional proposals with periodic molecular dynamics (MD) relaxation under harmonic backbone restraints. Receptor ensembles generated from an apo structure were evaluated against 859 experimental complexes from the OpenBind 2A protease benchmark and compared with the apo receptor and ensembles generated by restrained and unrestrained MD. With regular-space representative selection, MCMC recovered a ligand pose within 2 [A] of the experimental pose for 74.4% of complexes, compared with 51.0% for apo and 59.5% for restrained MD. Median minimum ligand heavy-atom RMSD decreased from 1.96 [A] for apo and 1.82 [A] for restrained MD to 1.62 [A] for MCMC. The largest gains occurred for complexes with greater side-chain displacement relative to pocket backbone displacement, consistent with the motions targeted by the protocol. MCMC representatives retained pocket geometries within the experimentally observed range, whereas unrestrained-MD representatives exhibited reduced pocket free volume and poor recovery. These findings support targeted side-chain sampling as a practical approach to generating apo-derived docking ensembles. The reported improvements measure best-case pose coverage across generated poses and receptors; their extension to prospective pose ranking and virtual screening remains to be established.

papers.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
papers.abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

papers.title: Interpreting graph neural networks reveals microbial association patterns in inflammatory bowel diseases
papers.abstract: Traditional machine learning models trained on gut microbiome abundance profiles can distinguish individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from non-IBD individuals. However, their interpretation typically considers taxa in isolation, making it difficult to understand how associations between taxa contribute to predictions. Here, we inferred individual-specific microbial association networks from longitudinal metagenomics data of 106 individuals in HMP2/iHMP and used them to train and interpret graph neural network (GNN) models, which we compared with abundance-based models such as Random Forest (RF). Although RF achieved higher predictive performance (AUPRC ~0.59 vs 0.446), interpreting the GNNs revealed that their predictions relied on a densely connected module of co-abundant Bacteroidales species. Unlike the taxa prioritized by RF, these species were not differentially abundant between conditions. In an independent cohort, this module carried most of the predictive signal, and removing its associations reduced performance to near chance. These results show that coordinated association structure, rather than abundance shifts alone, is a feature of the IBD gut microbiome, and that interpreting GNNs can uncover such patterns that complement abundance-based analyses.

papers.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS
papers.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

papers.title: The Quagmire of Immunogenicity-Guided Antibody Design: Labels Limit Progress
papers.abstract: Generative sequence-based antibody design is increasingly steered by learned property predictors, so a design objective is only as well specified as the labels behind its oracle. Immunogenicity is among the most clinically consequential properties to condition on, and among the least well specified: the supervisory signal is a single anti-drug-antibody percentage (ADA%) per molecule, aggregated from published trials. To analyze that signal, we first extended and corrected the widely used 217-entry dataset to 231 therapeutics with paired sequences, spanning formats from mouse to fully human. Then, we manually reconstructed the clinical evidence for 110 of them from primary sources. We find that an antibody format lookup outperforms every sequence-based learned predictor on the 231-antibody dataset. Apparent accuracy tracks the format composition of the evaluation split rather than sequence signal. Furthermore, the labels understate their own evidence: molecules labeled at [≤]6 ADA% span up to 86% across trials. We recomputed labels from the trial-level measurements and found that the advantage of the format-based approach disappears, while the sequence-based predictors degrade less under the cohort-weighted mean. We conclude that progress is limited by the label itself, and recommend reporting ADA% at the trial level, treating the target as a distribution rather than a point value, and evaluating against a format-based baseline.

papers.title: FateDriver: Weakly supervised dual-view graph learning for transition-specific prioritization of candidate regulators in cellular reprogramming
papers.abstract: Cellular reprogramming supports regenerative medicine, yet the endogenous regulators of a specified source-to-target transition remain incompletely defined. Existing computational methods rank candidate regulators from network topology, trajectory dynamics, or cell-state labels, leaving unused the factors experimentally delivered to induce the transition. We present FateDriver, a weakly supervised dual-view graph neural network that jointly represents cells and genes from single-cell transcriptomes, treats the delivered factors as sparse gene-level labels, and ranks the remaining genes for a specified transition under a positive--unlabeled formulation. Across two OSKM datasets and one GMT dataset, FateDriver ranked first or second among six methods in recovering externally curated reference genes, exceeded a supervision-matched non-graph model despite weaker co-expression with the delivered factors, and achieved the highest recovery of protein targets of pluripotency-inducing chemical cocktails in both OSKM datasets. Holding either the source or the endpoint fixed yielded distinct candidate programs, including a DDX58--interferon axis associated with cells lacking endogenous pluripotency markers. Applying the same framework to candidate source--target pairs prioritized distinct candidate origins for two in vivo partially reprogrammed intestinal populations. FateDriver converts sparse experimental knowledge into transition-specific hypotheses for regulator prioritization from single-cell trajectories.

papers.title: Pycea: a scverse toolkit for single-cell lineage tracing analysis
papers.abstract: Lineage tracing enables reconstruction of cellular histories in development, regeneration, and disease, but integrating lineage data into single-cell analysis workflows remains challenging. We introduce Pycea, a Python toolkit for lineage analysis and visualization, and TreeData, an extension of AnnData that stores lineage trees alongside cellular measurements. TreeData is compatible with Scanpy and other scverse tools, enabling integrated analysis without converting between formats. Pycea provides scalable methods for tree visualization, clade identification, distance comparisons, ancestral state inference, and lineage statistics. This software is open source and available at https://github.com/YosefLab/pycea.

papers.title: Cross-modal transfer enables zero-shot prediction of drug responses across cell types
papers.abstract: Genetic perturbation responses capture the functional consequences of gene-level interventions, providing functional information for drug-response prediction beyond baseline gene expression. Within the same cellular context, genetic and chemical perturbations engage shared regulatory networks, providing a biological basis for transferring response information between perturbation modalities. Here we introduce GRAFT, a framework that combines genetic-to-chemical transfer with cross-context prediction to infer drug-induced transcriptional responses without drug measurements in the target context. Across benchmarked LINCS and external contexts, GRAFT improved response correlation, directional agreement and magnitude reconstruction over competing methods, particularly for drugs with context-dependent responses. GRAFT-Adapt further refines predictions of unmeasured responses using a small number of drug measurements from the target context. GRAFT-Atlas spans 13 cellular contexts and 7,856 drug catalog entries, comprising 102,128 predictions for drug-context combinations. The atlas captured recognizable pharmacological neighborhoods, shared functional programs, context-dependent transcriptional changes and structural-functional associations supported by molecular docking. Across ten iPSC lines from distinct donors, GRAFT identified candidate inter-donor differences, with functional support for selected candidates from measured genetic perturbation responses. Together, GRAFT enables perturbation-informed prediction and comparison of drug responses across cellular contexts.

papers.title: tWhEEL: a transcript-aware workflow for quantifying CRISPR knockout feasibility using transcriptome assembly
papers.abstract: Gene redundancy can complicate loss-of-function experiments (knockout), and its extent varies among organisms and biological functions. Relating variation in gene redundancy to the availability of genome-editing targets can help researchers select tractable biological functions and experimental organisms. Here, we present the transcript-aware Whole-genomic Evaluation for Editing Locus (tWhEEL), a pipeline that infers redundancy in silico from transcript information and cross-references it with specific guide RNA designs. tWhEEL integrates CRISPR-Cas9 guide design with Gene Ontology (GO) and pathway annotations to compute a knockout feasibility index (KFI) for individual genes and functional categories. Interactive HTML reports link GO-associated KFI and pathway-associated KFI summaries to the contributing groups, genes, and guide candidates with links to QuickGO or WikiPathways. By linking sequence-level guide candidates to functional-level targetability, tWhEEL can support the selection of biological functions and organisms for reverse-genetic experiments. Applications to model and nonmodel datasets revealed distinct targetability profiles, including high full targetability in yeast and query-protein-set dependence in zebrafish. A zebrafish Fanconi anemia case study recovered 14 of 19 published target-site designs. By connecting sequence-level guide candidates with function-level experimental planning, tWhEEL provides a framework for comparing reverse genetic tractability and prioritizing biological functions and organisms for further study.

papers.title: Transcript quantification using context-aware MAPQ modeling
papers.abstract: Long-read RNA-sequencing enables accurate transcript-level quantification, but prior static filtering of MAPping Quality (MAPQ) can ignore transcriptome-intrinsic ambiguity, and discarding reads on this basis distorts abundance estimates. We present CALMeR (Context-Aware Long-read MAPQ-based Rescuer), which conditions MAPQ filtering on transcript properties rather than a fixed cutoff. CALMeR fits a zero-one inflated beta regression on various transcript and read-level features to model the expected MAPQ distribution for each alignment. Reads whose MAPQ fits this context, such as low-MAPQ reads from multi-isoform genes and paralog families are retained; reads with anomalously low MAPQ are removed as likely artifacts. Retained reads can be summed per transcript or passed to any downstream quantifier. Compared with a MAPQ [≥] 1 filter and expectation-maximization-based transcript quantification methods, CALMeR recovers more spike-in transcripts and better matches known spike-in concentrations. CALMeR is available at https://github.com/sparthib/CALMeR.

papers.title: Bioactivity foundation model for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization from sequence data
papers.abstract: Learning from large-scale bioactivity archives is complicated by heterogeneous assay readouts and differences in data reliability. Here we show that a model that predicts probability distributions over binding affinities from sequence data opens model training to vast and diverse troves of heterogeneous bioactivity data. We develop PSICHIC+, a bioactivity foundation model trained on approximately 82 million protein-ligand records using a distributional objective that preserves quantitative resolution while incorporating variation in data reliability. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, PSICHIC+ predicts binding affinity in milliseconds. In zero-shot virtual-screening benchmarks without target-specific training data, it improves enrichment over regression- and classification-based approaches and performs competitively with leading structure-based methods. In lab-in-the-loop campaigns, distribution-guided acquisition improves recovery of high-activity compounds under fixed screening budgets. Combining PSICHIC+ with Boltz-2 improves hit-to-lead affinity prediction over Boltz-2 alone, with mean correlation approaching that of FEP+ on the evaluated benchmarks, without requiring high-resolution protein structures. These results support distributional learning as a scalable approach to using heterogeneous bioactivity data for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization.

papers.title: EpiRank: partner-agnostic surface-patch retrieval for epitope prediction of protein binding interfaces
papers.abstract: Structure-based interface predictors are normally reported as a single pooled ROC AUC over a residue test set. For a protein designer the operative question is different and much harder: given one target chain, will the top-ranked surface patch be a real binding site? We built EpiRank, a partner-agnostic epitope predictor, on HumanPPI 29,246 predicted human dimers, 12,296 target chains, 4.18 M residues using only single-chain geometry and physicochemistry (170 features, no partner, no sequence search, no structural alphabet), and evaluated it as a retrieval problem with homology- and partner-graph-controlled splits, on the 3,529 chains that survive an explicit partner-contamination filter. The model places a real epitope in its top-ranked patch 64 % of the time. That number is far less informative than it looks. Compact patches placed at random hit a real epitope 41 % of the time under the same rule, so the model's lift is 1.57 x, not 64 %; 54 % of all predicted patches land on nothing; and when the same chains are scored by models trained on a 2,000-chain and an 11,669-chain superset, a substantial fraction change answer while the aggregate barely moves. We document four specific ways this task invites overstatement partner-graph percolation across splits, single-linkage homology percolation at the conventional 30 % identity threshold, a count-only hit rule that rewards spatial smoothing rather than signal, and hotspot precision conditioned on success, which ranks a random baseline above the trained model. Each was hit during development and each inverted a conclusion we had already drawn. We argue that interface-prediction papers should report lift over a geometry-matched random baseline, patch precision, and per-target stability alongside AUC, and we release the evaluation harness that computes them.

papers.title: Structure-resolved fold annotation of the medicinal-leech salivary-EV cargo: a Ly-6/uPAR three-finger scaffold and a structurally dark fraction
papers.abstract: Many proteins that medicinal leeches package into salivary extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry no interpretable sequence annotation, so the least-characterised part of a pharmacologically important secretome lacks even a fold assignment. A companion Astral-DIA study of Hirudinaria manillensis nominated 17 ultra-enriched candidate EV cargo proteins. Here we ask whether structure prediction and structural search can assign folds where sequence methods fail, and which candidates remain unresolved under prespecified criteria. With an offline pipeline (ESMFold, TM-align, Foldseek against AFDB-SwissProt and PDB100, UniRef90 search, protein-to-genome alignment), the candidates separate into intracellular/membrane machinery and a secreted, cysteine-dense fraction of three proteins with no Pfam domain. The predicted structure of the leech Protein-sleepless homolog g21166 supports its assignment to the Ly-6/uPAR three-finger fold (TM 0.58 vs CD59; best significant PDB match Lynx1); no function is inferred. g436 and g20791 returned no match meeting the criterion (alnTM [≥] 0.5, E [≤] 0.05) in either database, g436 even after homolog-informed modelling. Gene structure and splice junctions support a conserved locus for the two-Trypsin-segment model g8114 (catalytic unit not established). A Boltz-2 thrombin pilot did not support target engagement, and a pre-registered nicotinic test was terminated as undecidable. The results yield a structure-informed shortlist for experimental follow-up.

papers.title: In silico codon optimization and phylogenetic analysis of various strains of Sapovirus
papers.abstract: Introduction: Sapovirus (SaV) is an emerging enteric pathogen of rising public health importance, responsible for acute gastroenteritis in people of all ages and most often in children under five. Its genome is approximately 7.1-7.7 kb long, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, comprising two principal open reading frames; processing of the ORF1 product yields seven non-structural proteins and the major capsid protein VP1, while ORF2 encodes the minor structural protein VP2. Given the absence of therapies or an approved vaccine and the low yields of recombinant capsid protein, improving expression remains a priority. Methods: VP1 and VP2 sequences from twelve selected human SaV strains were aligned, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed by maximum likelihood method under the Tamura-Nei model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates, and both genes were optimized in silico for Escherichia coli using the OPTIMIZER. Results: The trees resolved three genogroups, GI, GII and GV, each strain placed alike by both genes. Every optimized sequence reached the ceiling value of 1.000 for the codon adaptation index (CAI). Mean CAI and GC% increased by 3.07 (207.0%) and 1.11 (11.1%) fold for VP1, and 3.11 (210.9%) and 1.14 (14.1%) fold for VP2, while AT% decreased. All changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001) and the encoded amino acid sequences were unaltered. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that Optmization raised host-matched codon usage in both capsid genes with no truncated proteins produced. The redesigned VP1 and VP2 sequences warrant further investigation as potential candidates for biotherapeutic and vaccine development. KEYWORDS: Sapovirus,CAI, codon optimization, VP1 capsid protein, GC content, DNA, phylogenetic analysis, vaccines

papers.title: Single-cell foundation models transfer across deep evolutionary distances
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are trained mostly on human and other vertebrate cells, yet are proposed as general-purpose models. Whether they transfer far beyond their training species is unknown. We evaluated zero-shot embeddings from Geneformer, scGPT and UCE against PCA and scVI in developmental atlases of Dictyostelium discoideum and Caenorhabditis elegans, separated from humans by 1.2 billion and 600 million years. Without retraining, the models recovered developmental order and preserved organism-specific cell identities. UCE encodes genes by protein sequence and could use 97% of measured genes, whereas Geneformer and scGPT, after ortholog mapping, used under one-fifth. UCE performed most consistently, often exceeding species-native baselines. Restricted to ortholog-mappable genes, it still scored above vocabulary-based models on five of six annotation tasks, some narrowly. Foundation models can thus yield informative cell embeddings across more than a billion years of evolution, and protein-sequence gene representations make these embeddings more complete and often more accurate.

papers.title: EMBER: Contextualized gene representations enable compositional prediction across cellular perturbations
papers.abstract: Predicting the effects of individual and combined perturbations is central to identifying context-specific vulnerabilities and designing targeted interventions. Yet learning gene representations that integrate functional relationships with cellular state and transfer across perturbation tasks remains challenging. Here, we present EMBER, a gene-centric foundation model that learns context-dependent functional representations of genes. EMBER combines interaction-guided contrastive learning with masked expression reconstruction during pretraining on a single-cell corpus curated for diversity and balanced sampling across cell types and experimental batches. EMBER decouples gene representation learning from task-specific prediction through a composable embedding framework: the pretrained encoder remains frozen, while lightweight probes combine contextualized gene embeddings to predict individual and combined perturbation effects. The same pretrained representations support single-gene perturbation-response prediction, digenic interaction prediction, and multi-target drug-response prediction. EMBER improves cross-context perturbation-response prediction and genetic-interaction ranking relative to evaluated baselines. EMBER also prioritized SCFD1, a mediator of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as a candidate dependency during mTOR inhibition. Together, these results establish contextualized gene embeddings as reusable building blocks for modeling genetic and pharmacological perturbations, supporting the prioritization of genetic interactions and context-specific interventions for experimental testing.

papers.title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
papers.abstract: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

papers.title: A comprehensive map of the sequence basis of transcription initiation in humans
papers.abstract: Transcription initiation is a key marker of active enhancers and promoters. Here we describe an atlas of efficient and interpretable deep learning models trained on over 200 transcription initiation profiling experiments representing all major human organs and many cancer types. We show that our models accurately predict initiation patterns from local DNA sequence and decode their sequence determinants across diverse cellular contexts.

papers.title: smoothclust: Spatial smoothing and boundary-density summaries for spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the measurement of gene expression while preserving tissue organization. A common analysis task is the identification of spatial domains, defined here as spatially coherent regions with consistent expression profiles or cell-type mixtures and represented using categorical spatial tissue maps. However, while numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial domains, interpretable summary measures to quantify spatial domain organization and tissue architecture at the sample level remain less standardized. Here, we present smoothclust, a framework for spatial domain analysis consisting of two components: a spatial-smoothing-based clustering workflow for generating spatial domain labels, and a boundary density (BD) metric that provides local and sample-level summaries of label transitions on a spatial graph. Building on established categorical spatial statistics, the raw BD metric is calculated from the proportion of neighboring spatial locations that are assigned to different domain labels, and requires only spatial coordinates and domain labels as inputs. The metric can be calculated using either our spatial-smoothing-based domain labels or labels from external clustering methods or manual annotations. Relative BD is a composition-adjusted summary, calculated by dividing raw BD by its expectation under random relabeling with the observed label counts. By quantifying label transitions, our framework translates spatial domain label maps into interpretable local and sample-level summary measures of tissue architecture, facilitating exploratory analyses and comparisons across samples and biological conditions. We demonstrate the approach through evaluations across datasets from several spatial transcriptomics platforms and simulations. The spatial-smoothing workflow and BD metric are implemented in the smoothclust R package, which is freely available from Bioconductor and GitHub.

papers.title: Serum nutritional-metabolic recovery during tuberculosis treatment across BMI-defined undernutrition strata: A longitudinal proteomic reanalysis
papers.abstract: Background Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and undernutrition is a major modifiable risk factor. Serum proteomics can capture systemic host recovery during therapy, but whether baseline BMI-defined undernutrition alters this trajectory is unclear. Methods We reanalysed processed longitudinal tandem-mass-tag serum proteomics from 30 adults with pulmonary tuberculosis and durable cure sampled at baseline and weeks 8, 17, 26 and 52. Thirteen participants had baseline BMI =18.5 kg/m2. Protein-level analyses evaluated baseline differences and week-specific within-participant change; module and recovery-axis models evaluated BMI-by-time interactions, with random-intercept mixed models added as a repeated-measures sensitivity analysis. Three complementary treatment-responsive modules were integrated into an exploratory, nonredundant 36-protein nutritional-metabolic summary axis. Results The reconstructed dataset contained 1,923 quantified features across 150 participant-visits. Inflammatory/acute-phase and metal-handling/nutritional-immunity module scores declined during follow-up, whereas lipid/apolipoprotein-transport, nutritional-carrier and endocrine-immunometabolic scores increased. In the primary week-specific paired-change analyses, no protein-level between-BMI difference in longitudinal change survived false-discovery-rate correction; no curated-module BMI-by-time interaction survived correction. The 36-protein summary axis increased in both BMI strata from week 17 onward. In a random-intercept model without interaction, the BMI =18.5 kg/m2 comparison stratum, although the confidence interval included zero (difference -1.34, 95% CI -2.76 to 0.08; p = .064). Categorical and continuous BMI-by-time interaction tests did not detect differential axis trajectories. Conclusions Tuberculosis treatment was accompanied by broad longitudinal remodelling of circulating inflammatory and nutritional-metabolic protein systems. An exploratory 36-protein summary axis increased in both baseline BMI strata, while formal interaction tests did not detect BMI-dependent trajectories and remained too imprecise to establish equivalence. BMI should be regarded as an anthropometric proxy rather than a comprehensive measure of nutritional state. The defined axis provides a framework for prospective validation alongside direct measures of body composition, micronutrients, treatment exposure and clinical outcomes.
